title: Holmes Freak Murder Case
notes: Recurring detective-cast nodes (Conan, Heiji Hattori, Ran, Kogoro Mouri) omitted by convention even though Heiji is the guest deducer this episode. Three linked incidents at the isolated Mycroft Lodge, all committed by the same culprit: (1) owner Kanaya killed and his corpse rigged to 'drive itself' off a cliff using a rigor-mortis/heater trick, (2) a second car in the garage rigged as a gasoline-fume trap originally meant for Fujisawa but which killed Ayako Oki instead when she searched it independently, (3) a staged blackout during which Fujisawa was attacked with an ice pick and survived. No event nodes: every action is a directly typed edge between the entities involved, sharing an order integer. Two red-herring has_motive_against/implicates edges are included (Kawatsu via the coffee-pack wire, Toda via Kogoro's joking hypnosis theory) since Heiji's live deduction visibly considers and discards both before landing on the true culprit. case_type: murder.

clues.desc: Standard rigor mortis (onset 30min-2h, full rigidity by 9-12h, loosening from ~30h, gone by ~70h) doesn't fit the timeline unless heat is factored in: at roughly 35 degrees C the loosening accelerates to 24-30h, which matches the owner vanishing after 10 PM two nights before and the car moving on its own about 29 hours later, near 3:30 AM -- pins the killing to shortly after he vanished and proves only someone absent from the group after dinner that night could have staged it.

The living-room chair used to escape through the smashed window was found neatly pushed back under the table with glass shards still in it -- no one fleeing outside stops to tidy furniture, so the killer never left the room and staged the break-in from inside, hiding the chair only to wipe fingerprints off later.

Heiji invents a fake question #241 ("what did the Dancing Men code say to the killer?") that never appeared on the real 1000-question test; Kento confidently 'recalls' answering it. Since Ayako had already seen his real copy sitting blank, his confident answer to a nonexistent question proves he never filled it out because he already knew Kanaya, the grader, was dead.
